title: Proof pages for an independent school
metaTitle: Proof pages for an independent school
excerpt: Show a real constraint, the decision it forced, and students in the day. Close with a visit or an inquiry for a family in a similar spot.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table, many small claims competing for one glance.
caption: A home screen full of icons is noise. A proof page should be one decision, clearly shown. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What counts as proof on a school site?
faqs.answer: A constraint families will meet, the choice you made because of it, and photographs of students in that day. A shared yard, a house stair, or one class teacher all year are real subjects. A crest and an empty lawn are not.

faqs.question: How should children appear?
faqs.answer: As a group at work, with the size of the class visible, under consent you already require. Skip full names on public portraits. Skip a frame that only works by embarrassing a child. Caption the year group, the activity, and the term.

faqs.question: How should the page end?
faqs.answer: Invite a similar family to visit that age, or to inquire with the child's year. Restate the constraint in the closing line. If a year is full, say so. Link the fee page if cost is part of the same decision.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An independent school case study page should show a constraint, a decision, and students in the day, not a crest. A parent deciding where a child will spend years does not need a gallery of empty rooms or a screenshot of a prospectus. They need to see how the school handles a real limit, and then a way to visit or inquire if their child is in a similar spot.

Google's people-first guidance asks for original information and for evidence of first-hand experience, not a rewrite of what every school says about nurturing potential. A proof page is where that standard becomes practical. Nielsen Norman Group's finding that people read only about a quarter of the text is the other constraint: the proof has to be graspable without a long commemorative essay, or it will not be read past the first picture.

## What counts as proof

Proof is not a testimonial slider and not an inspection badge on its own. Proof is a specific situation your school has already faced, told so a stranger can judge the result. The situation might be a small hall and how assembly actually works. It might be mixed ages on one stair. It might be the decision to keep one class teacher all year instead of a specialist carousel you cannot staff well.

The reader is a parent, not an awards jury. They are asking: if my child is here, will the difficult thing about this school be handled with judgment, or with camouflage? The page answers with the day, not with a narrative about your brand.

One page can carry one situation. A second situation can be a second page, later, if you truly have a second decision to show. A school does not need a case study for every subject. It needs one that tells the truth about the constraint families actually meet.

Call the page by the situation. "A year 4 morning" is a better title than "Our transformation story." The parent needs the day. Save institutional language for the footer.

## Name the constraint

Open with the limit, in the first paragraph. The hall cannot hold every child on chairs. The building is a house, and the science you can offer is a bench at the back of a classroom until a named age. You have no bus. You do not select by exam, so the class contains a wide spread and the teaching has to meet it. The playground is one yard, shared, with a rota.

A constraint stated early is a sign of confidence. It also filters. The family that needs a large sports academy can leave before a child has invested hope. The family that wants a known adult and a short walk can stay and read how you dealt with the small yard. Both are correct uses of the page.

Do not begin with a triumph. "We reimagined education" tells the reader you plan to sell them past the problem. Lead with the measurement they will notice on a visit: the count in the room, the hour the yard is theirs, the stair, the absence of a thing other schools advertise.

If the constraint is seasonal, say the season. The yard in June is not the yard in February. A proof page that only shows sports day is a partial truth. Give the wet Tuesday one honest sentence and one photograph, or do not claim the day is the same all year.

Avoid a constraint that is a humblebrag. "Our challenge is that families love us so much." That is not a constraint. The single yard is a constraint. The one-room library is a constraint. Stay with rooms, hours, and numbers you can check.

## Show the decision

A decision is a choice you made because of the constraint, including a choice to leave something alone. We did not pretend the hall is a theatre. We sit the youngest on the floor and keep assembly short. We stopped advertising a parade of specialist subjects in the junior years because the class teacher is the point. We publish the yard rota instead of a drone shot that makes one yard look like a campus.

The decision should be specific enough that another school could not copy the paragraph by swapping the crest. If your text works for any independent school, it is not a decision. It is a tone.

Explain the option you rejected. Rejecting the wide-angle photograph of the yard. Rejecting an entrance test that would have made the brochure easier and the mission false. Rejecting a claim of "extensive labs." The rejection is the proof that someone thought. A before-and-after that only celebrates a new logo is an advertisement for the redesign, not for the childhood.

If a head, a teacher, or a governor made the call, name the role. First-hand experience is the standard in Google's guidance, and it is what a parent believes. "We decided" is weaker than "The year-4 teacher asked us to stop promising a silent library, because the library is the corridor outside her room."

Keep the decision at the scale of the child. A proof page about your rebrand, your new website, or your capital campaign serves the institution's feelings. Those stories can live in a board paper. Here, the decision has to change the day.

## Students and the day, not a crest

Then show the students. Not the shield, not the empty chapel, not a lawn with no one on it, not a child hired from a library of photographs. The class working, the lunch table with the number of seats you really have, the gate at pickup with the adult who is actually there. Two or three photographs are enough if they agree. Twelve frames that hunt for an angle with better light are a sign you do not trust the day.

Write a caption a parent could use as a checklist. "Year 4, Tuesday morning, about eighteen children, class teacher at the board, October." Captions are part of the proof. A caption that says "inspiring minds" is a retreat.

If a parent has written something useful, use one sentence that mentions the constraint, with permission, and without exposing the child. "The yard is small, and our daughter knows which break is hers." That sentence supports the decision. "Best school ever" could be pasted onto any site. It is not proof.

Say who this day is for, and who it is not for. A child who will do well with one main teacher and a short walk. Not a child whose week depends on a squad, a pool, or a subject you do not teach. The recommendation is the page's conclusion. Make it narrow enough to be true.

Protect children in the way you already should. No full names on public portraits. No moment that embarrasses a child for the sake of a vivid frame. Proof is not extraction. If a photograph only works by making a child a prop, it does not go on the page.

## Why a gallery without a decision fails

A row of handsome frames with no constraint and no choice is decoration. It asks the parent to feel something and does not help them decide. Every school in the other tabs has a feeling and a crest. The decision is rarer.

Screenshots of your prospectus, your social grid, or your admissions portal are the wrong objects. The child will not spend years inside your PDF. If a designer wants a process gallery, keep it for the internal review. Publish the day.

Quotes without a situation fail in the same way. Praise with no Tuesday in it is not proof. If you cannot attach the quote to the constraint, leave it off this page.

A film that glides past the difficult stair and opens on the shield is a gallery in motion. If you use moving images, hold on the constraint long enough to read a caption. Do not score it with music that tells the parent what to feel before they have counted the children in the room.

Ask a friend who is a parent to look for thirty seconds and name the decision. If they describe a mood and cannot name the choice, the page is still a lookbook. Add the sentence where you rejected the exam, or the fake lab, or the wide-angle yard. Then ask again.

## End on a similar family's visit

Close by telling a similar family how to act. If this is the day they want, book a visit for that age, or inquire with the child's year if they cannot visit yet. Sending everyone to a generic form undoes the care of the page. The family that just accepted the small yard should not be funneled into a different campus story you do not have.

Restate the constraint in the closing line so it travels with them. "Visit a junior open morning if one class teacher and a shared yard are what you want." That sentence is the page in miniature. A similar family can use it. A mismatched family can leave without a heartfelt rejection later, which saves the office and spares the child a confusing tour.

Do not invent scarcity. "Only a few places left" as a style, when it is not specifically true of a year, trains families to distrust you. If a year is full, say the year is full, and say whether a visit is still useful or whether it would waste their hope. Honesty about a closed year is a decision, and it belongs in the closing.

Link fees if the cost of this stage surprises people. Proof without the shape of the fee is an unfinished argument for a years-long choice. You do not need to paste the table. You need a path to it.

## How many of these you need

Start with one. Publish it when the photographs match the sentences and the children are protected. Add another only when a second constraint produces a different decision. Two pages that say "community" in different adjectives are worse than one. Parents can tell when a school has started a content program instead of a record.

Keep the page current when the day changes. A new teacher pattern, a yard that became a building site, a class size that grew. Proof that is out of date becomes a complaint at the gate. Put the term on the page and update it when you recheck the facts.

Give the page a place a parent can find, under the age it describes, not under a news archive. A true page that cannot be reached does not help the comparison. [How the menu should point at the jobs a parent came to do](/blog/navigation-for-an-independent-school) follows from here. The label can say "The day." The page still has to be findable in one tap.

To see work that keeps a clear decision on the page, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The order is the constraint, the decision, and the students, then a visit.
